title: Iberian Peninsula
wiki_lead:
The Iberian Peninsula (IPA:  eye-BEER-ee-ən), also known as Iberia, is a peninsula in southwestern Europe. 
Mostly separated from the rest of continental Europe by the Pyrenees, the Iberian Peninsula includes Peninsular Spain and Continental Portugal, which together make up almost all of the region, as well as Andorra, Gibraltar, and a small part of Metropolitan France. With an area of approximately 583,254 square kilometres (225,196 sq mi), and a population of roughly 53 million, it is the second-largest European peninsula by area, after the Scandinavian Peninsula.

The Iberian Peninsula (IPA:  eye-BEER-ee-ən), also known as Iberia, is a peninsula in southwestern Europe. 
Mostly separated from the rest of continental Europe by the Pyrenees, the Iberian Peninsula includes Peninsular Spain and Continental Portugal, which together make up almost all of the region, as well as Andorra, Gibraltar, and a small part of Metropolitan France. With an area of approximately 583,254 square kilometres (225,196 sq mi), and a population of roughly 53 million, it is the second-largest European peninsula by area, after the Scandinavian Peninsula.


Etymology

The Iberian Peninsula has always been associated with the River Ebro (Ibēros in ancient Greek and Ibērus or Hibērus in Latin). The association was so well known it was hardly necessary to state. For example, Ibēria was the country "this side of the Ibērus" in Strabo. Pliny goes so far as to assert that the Greeks had called "the whole of the peninsula" Hiberia because of the Hiberus River. 
The river appears in the Ebro Treaty of 226 BCE between Rome and Carthage, setting the limit of Carthaginian interest at the Ebro. The fullest description of the treaty, stated in Appian, uses Ibērus. With reference to this border, Polybius states that the "native name" is Ibēr, apparently the original word, stripped of its Greek or Latin -os or -us termination.
The early range of these natives, which geographers and historians place from the present southern Spain to the present southern France along the Mediterranean coast, is marked by instances of a readable script expressing a yet unknown language, dubbed "Iberian". Whether this was the native name or was given to them by the Greeks for their residence near the Ebro remains unknown. Credence in Polybius imposes certain limitations on etymologizing: if the language remains unknown, the meanings of the words, including Iber, must also remain unknown. 
In modern Basque, the word ibar means "valley" or "watered meadow", while ibai means "river", but there is no proof connecting the names with Ebro or Iberia.


Greek name
The word Iberia comes from the Latin word Hiberia originating from the Ancient Greek word Ἰβηρία (Ibēríā), used by Greek geographers under the rule of the Roman Empire to refer to what is known today in English as the Iberian Peninsula. At that time, the name did not describe a single geographical entity or a distinct population; the same name was used for the Kingdom of Iberia, natively known as Kartli in the Caucasus, the core region of what would later become the Kingdom of Georgia. 
It was Strabo who first reported the delineation of Iberia from Gaul (Keltikē) by the Pyrenees and included the entire land mass southwest (he says "west") from there. With the fall of the Western Roman Empire and the consolidation of Romance languages, the word "Iberia" continued the Roman word Hiberia and the Greek word Ἰβηρία.
Hecataeus of Miletus was the first known to use the term Iberia, which he wrote about c. 500 BCE. Herodotus of Halicarnassus says of the Phocaeans that "it was they who made the Greeks acquainted with [...] Iberia." According to Strabo, prior historians used Iberia to mean the country "this side of the Ἶβηρος (Ibēros, the Ebro) as far north as the Rhône, but in his day they set the Pyrenees as the limit. Polybius respects that limit, but identifies Iberia as the Mediterranean side as far south as Gibraltar, with the Atlantic side having no name. Elsewhere he says that Saguntum is "on the seaward foot of the range of hills connecting Iberia and Celtiberia."


Roman names

According to Charles Ebel, the ancient sources in both Latin and Greek use Hispania and Hiberia (Greek: Iberia) as synonyms. The confusion of the words was because of an overlapping in political and geographic perspectives. The Latin word Hiberia, similar to the Greek Iberia, literally translates to "land of the Hiberians". This word was derived from the river Hiberus, now called Ebro or Ebre. Hiber (Iberian) was thus used
grok_lead: The Iberian Peninsula constitutes the southwestern promontory of Europe, spanning approximately 583,254 square kilometers and supporting a population of approximately 58 million inhabitants, predominantly in the independent states of Spain and Portugal, with the enclaved microstate of Andorra and the British Overseas Territory of Gibraltar comprising the remainder. It ranks as the second-largest peninsula on the continent by area, after the Scandinavian Peninsula, and features a diverse topography dominated by the elevated Meseta central plateau, encircled by formidable mountain ranges such as the Pyrenees to the north, the Cantabrian Mountains to the northwest, and the Baetic System to the south. Bounded by the Atlantic Ocean along its western and southern coasts, the Mediterranean Sea to the east and southeast, and the Pyrenees forming a natural barrier against France, the peninsula's geography fosters varied climates ranging from Mediterranean in the east to oceanic in the northwest, influencing its agricultural productivity and settlement patterns. Major river systems, including the Douro, Tagus, Guadiana, and Ebro, originate in the interior highlands and flow toward the Atlantic or Mediterranean, supporting irrigation and hydropower while shaping fertile valleys amid otherwise arid plateaus. Approximately three-quarters of the land consists of this rugged, elevated terrain, contributing to seismic activity and resource distribution that have historically conditioned human adaptation and economic development. Politically unified under Roman, Visigothic, and later Iberian crowns following the protracted Reconquista against Muslim polities, the peninsula emerged as the launchpad for European overseas expansion in the 15th and 16th centuries, with Portugal and Spain establishing vast colonial empires that disseminated language, culture, and institutions across the Americas, Africa, and Asia. Today, it remains a nexus of economic integration within the European Union, marked by regional disparities, including denser populations along coastal corridors and ongoing debates over autonomy in areas like Catalonia and the Basque Country, while its strategic location continues to underpin trade and migration dynamics.
